<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\Bigg[\frac{(r_{t}-\mu_{\theta}(z_{t},a_{t}))^{2}}{2\sigma_{\theta}(z_{t},a_{t})^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\log\sigma_{\theta}(z_{t},a_{t})^{2}\Bigg]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="2.600em" minsize="2.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\Bigg[\frac{(r_{t}-\mu_{\theta}(z_{t},a_{t}))^{2}}{2\sigma_{\theta}(z_{t},a_{t})^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\log\sigma_{\theta}(z_{t},a_{t})^{2}\Bigg].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">In training process, the target rewards are the multi-step Monte Carlo return, i.e., <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the variance <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is scaled to <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\sigma_{\text{min}},\sigma_{\text{max}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\sigma_{\text{min}},\sigma_{\text{max}}]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{min}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{min}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{max}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> detailed in the Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Hyperparameter settings ‣ Appendix D Method Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The learned predictor <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{\theta}(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t};\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t};\omega)</annotation></semantics></math> leverages <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to estimate the conditional expectation of the target <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and leverages <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to characterize the scale of the stochastic residual under the given state and policy. By reparameterization, a predictive sample can be written as <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})=\mu_{\theta}+\sigma_{\theta}\odot\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})=\mu_{\theta}+\sigma_{\theta}\odot\xi</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)</annotation></semantics></math>, and hence admits the decomposition <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})=r_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})=r_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> collects the remaining approximation error <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}-r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}-r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and the stochastic component induced by <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. Due to the optimized tradeoff of the variance term in the denominator (in <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{rew}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>rew</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{rew}}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the enforced lower bound <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>, it implies a positive variance w.r.t <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, especially relevant in early learning, which thereby supports the <span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">variance</span> assumption required by Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Predictive Reward Prevents Degenerate Metric). ‣ 3.2 The Proposed Predictive Bisimulation Metric ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Non-degenerate Theoretical Analysis.</span> Next, we leverage Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Predictive Reward Prevents Degenerate Metric). ‣ 3.2 The Proposed Predictive Bisimulation Metric ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> to show that the bisimulation metric with the predictive reward yields a non-degenerate distance, thereby offering theoretical justification for learning a robust representation space under sparse reward conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.3</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Predictive Reward Prevents Degenerate Metric)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let the state space <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> be compact and the policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> fixed.
Consider the predictive bisimulation operator <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>π</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, the learned reward model satisfies
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})=r_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})=r_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon_{t}|s_{t},a_{t}]=\Sigma&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon_{t}|s_{t},a_{t}]=\Sigma&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, the unique fixed point <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{d}_{\text{pre}}=\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}\widetilde{d}_{\text{pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">pre</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">pre</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{d}_{\text{pre}}=\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}\widetilde{d}_{\text{pre}}</annotation></semantics></math>
admits a strictly positive expected diameter in the sparse-reward region
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{0}=\{s|r(s,a)=0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{0}=\{s|r(s,a)=0\}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\big[\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{S}_{0};\widetilde{d}_{\text{pre}})\big]\in\Big(0,\frac{c_{R}}{1-c_{T}}\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sqrt{\Sigma}\Big]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mi>diam</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">pre</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>π</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></msqrt></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\big[\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{S}_{0};\widetilde{d}_{\text{pre}})\big]\in\Big(0,\frac{c_{R}}{1-c_{T}}\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sqrt{\Sigma}\Big].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of Lemma <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Predictive Reward Prevents Degenerate Metric). ‣ 3.2 The Proposed Predictive Bisimulation Metric ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> is available in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 The Proof of the Predictive Reward Prevents Degenerate Metric ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>. This result formally shows that the predictive bisimulation employed in TEB preserves a nonzero geometric scale within the latent space. While the classical <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>-bisimulation metric collapses in sparse-reward environments because the reward differential <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|r^{\pi}_{s_{i}}-r^{\pi}_{s_{j}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>π</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|r^{\pi}_{s_{i}}-r^{\pi}_{s_{j}}|</annotation></semantics></math> vanishes, TEB’s predictive reward model introduces a stochastic residual <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> with finite variance <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. This residual induces a positive expected separation between latent states, thereby preventing the bisimulation metric from degenerating into a zero distance. Intuitively, the predictor’s uncertainty injects a minimal “energy floor” into the metric-based representation learning, which ensures that the encoder <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\omega}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>ω</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\omega}</annotation></semantics></math> continues to receive meaningful gradient signals and that the learned latent manifold remains well-structured even when external rewards are sparse or absent. In practice, this mechanism directly explains TEB’s empirical stability and strong generalization under sparse rewards.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Besides this, another situation also empirically favors the non-degenerate advantage of our predictive bisimulation metrics. Specifically, when individual rewards occur, the reward predictor can also leverage the network’s inductive and generalization abilities to ensure that many similar transitions generate positive rewards, thus enabling the sampled <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{\pi}_{R}(s_{i},s_{j})&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{\pi}_{R}(s_{i},s_{j})&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. This advantage mainly occurs in the early stages of training because the predictor has not yet overfitted. Nonetheless, the above is an empirical advantage we speculate on and do not focus on.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Loss.</span> Let <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{d}_{\omega}(s_{i},s_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>ω</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{d}_{\omega}(s_{i},s_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> be the approximated bisimulation metric distance <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\phi_{\omega}(s_{i})-\phi_{\omega}(s_{j})||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>ω</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>ω</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\phi_{\omega}(s_{i})-\phi_{\omega}(s_{j})||</annotation></semantics></math> between <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> parameterized by <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, we train the encoder by a bootstrapped bisimulation regression loss:</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{bisim}}(\omega)=\mathbb{E}_{s_{i},s_{j}\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\hat{d}_{\omega}(s_{i},s_{j})-\mathrm{sg}[\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}d_{\text{pre}}](s_{i},s_{j};\bar{\omega})\big)^{2}\Big]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>bisim</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>ω</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>sg</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>π</mi></msup><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>ω</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{bisim}}(\omega)=\mathbb{E}_{s_{i},s_{j}\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\hat{d}_{\omega}(s_{i},s_{j})-\mathrm{sg}[\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}d_{\text{pre}}](s_{i},s_{j};\bar{\omega})\big)^{2}\Big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>sg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]</annotation></semantics></math> denotes stop gradients with the frozen parameters, e.g. <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\omega}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ω</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\omega}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. In addition, we need to learn a dynamic transition model through common loss structure <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>dyn</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}}</annotation></semantics></math> following Chen et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and Pan, 2022</a>)</cite>. The overall representation objective is <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{\text{bisim}}+\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rew}}+\lambda_{p}\mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>rep</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>bisim</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>rew</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>dyn</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}}=\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{\text{bisim}}+\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rew}}+\lambda_{p}\mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the coefficients referenced from previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and Pan, 2022</a>)</cite> and detailed in the Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Hyperparameter settings ‣ Appendix D Method Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Metric-based Intrinsic Exploration</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Link to Intrinsic Exploration.</span>  The definition of the bisimulation metric directly indicates that it can measure behavioral similarity by constructing a distance based on the difference in rewards and the dynamic transition distribution between two states. This inspires us to utilize the property directly to measure the behavioral distance relevant to the task in the latent space <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>, and then to carefully design an intrinsic bonus based on this distance that can facilitate the exploration of reinforcement learning. Furthermore, an important characteristic of the connection between the bisimulation metrics and the value function further suggests the above insight.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.4</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Value Difference Bound)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Given states <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> be the state value function over policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, we have,</span></p>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{matrix}\left|V^{\pi}\left(s_{i}\right)-V^{\pi}\left(s_{j}\right)\right|\end{matrix}\leq\widetilde{d}_{pre}\left(s_{i},s_{j}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{matrix}\left|V^{\pi}\left(s_{i}\right)-V^{\pi}\left(s_{j}\right)\right|\end{matrix}\leq\widetilde{d}_{pre}\left(s_{i},s_{j}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem4" title="Theorem 3.4 (Value Difference Bound). ‣ 3.3 Metric-based Intrinsic Exploration ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a> is available in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 The Proof of the Value Difference Bound ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>. It shows that given any two states, their value function bound is held by predictive bisimulation metrics. In addition, the theory suggests that distant states in the metric possibly differ substantially in long-term value, while simultaneously increasing the probability of discovering high-value states. The feature also motivates us to construct meaningful exploration bonuses by the bisimulation metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metric-based Potential Function.</span> Nevertheless, using the metric itself as an intrinsic reward does not reliably reflect meaningful novelty, and it may encourage agents to make local transitions. Instead, we build a relative novelty signal via a potential function defined in the learned latent space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.3" class="ltx_p">First, we define a metric-based potential with <span id="S3.SS3.p4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">pseudo-state anchor</span> <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, which aims to potentially measure the absolute task-relevant novelty of the current state in a batch of samples with a batch size of <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>

<p id="S3.SS3.p4.4" class="ltx_p">with</p>
<table id="S3.E13" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E13X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E13X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r_{\star}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{k=1}^{B}\mathbf{r}_{(k)},~z^{\prime}_{\star}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{k=1}^{B}\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>B</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>B</mi></munderover></mstyle><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.497em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mo>⋆</mo><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>B</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>B</mi></munderover></mstyle><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r_{\star}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{k=1}^{B}\mathbf{r}_{(k)},~z^{\prime}_{\star}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{k=1}^{B}\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mo>⋆</mo><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the anchor reward and the latent anchor state averaged from batch transitions in the training stage, as well as <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{(k)}=\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(s_{k},a_{k};\bar{\omega})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>ω</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{(k)}=\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(s_{k},a_{k};\bar{\omega})</annotation></semantics></math>. Particularly, <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mo>⋆</mo><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> calculates the element-wise average of a batch of next latent state across hidden neurons. Therefore, we employ this abstract average information as anchors to approximate the global novelty of the current latent state.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">Then, we introduce potential-based shaping to compute the intrinsic exploration bonus between adjacent latent states. Specifically, it calculates the relative discounted distance between consecutive metric-based potentials as the intrinsic bonus, i.e., <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})</annotation></semantics></math>, thus producing a meaningful exploration bonus that approximates the novelty relevant to the global task.</p>
<table id="S3.E14" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E14X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E14X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle F(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle F(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E14X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\gamma\,\Phi(s_{t+1})-\Phi(s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\gamma\,\Phi(s_{t+1})-\Phi(s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E14Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\gamma\,d_{\text{pre}}(s_{t+1},s_{\star};\bar{\omega})-d_{\text{pre}}(s_{t},s_{\star};\bar{\omega})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>ω</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>ω</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\gamma\,d_{\text{pre}}(s_{t+1},s_{\star};\bar{\omega})-d_{\text{pre}}(s_{t},s_{\star};\bar{\omega}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.3" class="ltx_p">Finally, I define the intrinsic reward <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{int}=F(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{int}=F(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})</annotation></semantics></math> and a new reward function that aggregates the external rewards and the intrinsic reward, i.e., <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{\prime}=r+\eta\,r^{\text{int}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mtext>int</mtext></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{\prime}=r+\eta\,r^{\text{int}}</annotation></semantics></math>, to train the temporal difference loss. The selection of <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> can be found in the Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Hyperparameter settings ‣ Appendix D Method Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem5" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.5</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Policy Invariance of Metric-based Shaping)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r,\gamma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r,\gamma)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the original MDP, and consider the modified reward function <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{\prime}=r+\eta\,F(s,a,a^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{\prime}=r+\eta\,F(s,a,a^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> defined in Eq (<a href="#S3.E14" title="Equation 14 ‣ 3.3 Metric-based Intrinsic Exploration ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>). Then the modified MDP <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r^{\prime},\gamma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r^{\prime},\gamma)</annotation></semantics></math> with the metric-based potential preserves the optimal policy of <math id="S3.Thmtheorem5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> by,</span></p>
<table id="S3.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}^{*}(s,a)=Q_{\mathcal{M}}^{*}(s,a)-\eta\,\Phi(s),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal{S}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}^{*}(s,a)=Q_{\mathcal{M}}^{*}(s,a)-\eta\,\Phi(s),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal{S}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 3.5 (Policy Invariance of Metric-based Shaping). ‣ 3.3 Metric-based Intrinsic Exploration ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a> can be found in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 The Proof the Policy Invariance of Predicted Bisimulation Shaping ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>. The theorem shows that potential-based reward shaping does not change the optimal policy, since optimal action-value functions imply that <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\arg\max_{a}Q^{*}_{\mathcal{M^{\prime}}}(s,a)=\arg\max_{a}Q^{*}_{\mathcal{M}}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arg\max_{a}Q^{*}_{\mathcal{M^{\prime}}}(s,a)=\arg\max_{a}Q^{*}_{\mathcal{M}}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> is held. This conclusion demonstrates that intrinsic rewards based on potential functions can more stably transform the predictive bisimulation metric-based distances into value learning and convergence.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiment</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first compare TEB against powerful visual RL baselines on the challenging MetaWorld benchmark. We then evaluate its pure exploration ability on the Maze2D environment by comparing with recent exploration algorithms. Finally, we present qualitative visualizations and extensive ablation studies to further analyze the key components of TEB.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Environments.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MetaWorld is a challenging benchmark suite for visual robotic manipulation, detailed in the Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 MetaWorld Tasks ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>. In the setting, the agent acts from high-dimensional observations with visual distracting elements, and receives sparse and even success-based rewards. Maze2D is a low-dimensional continuous-control navigation benchmark with 2D maze layouts ranging from simple Corridors to hard Bottleneck task. The source code will be released later.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18724v1/mw_fig.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/271;" width="476" height="271"></object>

Each experiment runs with three random seeds, with shaded region representing the standard deviation across seeds.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18724v1/figures/vis_maze.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/186;" width="452" height="186" alt="Refer to caption">

<td id="S4.T1.5.1.8.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">0.40 <math id="S4.T1.m48" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> 0.02</td>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span>
In MetaWorld experiments, we conduct a broad comparison of TEB with the current strong visual RL algorithms: DrM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, CTRL-SR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and RAP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and Pan, 2022</a>)</cite>, and the representative exploration algorithms: ICM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pathak et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, CeSD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and LBS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazzaglia et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. All algorithms are on top of the DrQ-v2 framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yarats et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> except for CTRL-SR that follows the official framework. Specifically, CTRL-SR is a latest algorithm that alleviates representation and exploration difficulties through spectral representations. DrM facilitates policy learning in sparse reward environments by minimizing dormant ratios with visual settings. RAP is a strong algorithm with bisimulation metric-based representation learning. In the Maze environment, the comparative intrinsic exploration baselines consist of common exploration algorithms: LBS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazzaglia et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, RND <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burda et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, Disagreement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pathak et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, ICM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pathak et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, and ProtoRL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yarats et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, and 5 skill discovery baselines: CeSD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, BeCL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, LSD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, DIAYN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eysenbach et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, and SMM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, where CeSD is standard and state-of-the-art. More details on these baselines in the Appendix <a href="#A3.SS6" title="C.6 Baselines Details in Maze2D Experiments ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison Metrics.</span>
In MetaWorld, the success rate of each task is the metric for comparing all algorithms. We train different environment steps according to the difficulty of the task. In Maze2D, to quantify exploration ability, we compare the state coverage ratios of the policies over 100K environment steps, where the ratio measures the proportion of visited units to all units in a task map.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>MetaWorld Experiments</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments evaluate the ability of TEB in enabling task-aware exploration and learning effective policies from pixel observations. We consider six tasks of varying difficulty, e.g., hard <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stick-pull</span> and middle <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Box-close</span>. Note that even for the simpler <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Box-close</span>, learning an efficient policy remains non-trivial due to their sparse reward structure and significant visual distractions. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Environments. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, TEB consistently outperforms strong baseline methods across all tasks, which shows both faster convergence and higher success rates. In particular, on challenging tasks such as <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stick-pull</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Push-back</span>, TEB achieves success rates of 87.9% and 98.4% (the best success rates are in Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ C.2 MetaWorld Experiments ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> of the Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 MetaWorld Experiments ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>) and significantly surpasses all baselines, which empirically demonstrates its strong comprehensive performance in complex visual environments with sparse rewards. By contrast, among intrinsic exploration baselines, we observe that CeSD fails to obtain rewards and successfully complete tasks such as <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Push-back</span>. This likely due to the limitations of skill discovery–driven intrinsic rewards in challenging visual tasks. It is worth noting that the inverse dynamics model of ICM can also effectively filter out interfering elements, potentially providing strong support for more accurate exploration. Furthermore, CTRL-SR converges slowly in many tasks, such as the <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Push-back</span> task, and may even fail to learn a responsive policy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Reward-free Maze2D Experiments</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Maze2D tasks, our experiments aim to verify whether intrinsic rewards built on the predictive bisimulation metric can demonstrate efficient exploration abilities under reward-free settings. Note that since the Maze2D environment directly provides low-dimensional states, TEB does not train representation learning loss <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{bisim}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>bisim</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{bisim}}</annotation></semantics></math>, but instead directly measures a metric-based exploration bonus with states. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Environments. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, compared to existing exploration algorithms, TEB exhibits the strongest pure exploration capability, achieving the highest state coverage across various maze layouts, from simple corridors to complex bottlenecks. Specifically, using 100K steps as a benchmark, TEB shows a significant advantage over the previous best baseline algorithm, i.e., CeSD, in square maze series. For example, TEB achieves coverage scores of 0.87 and 0.85 on <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Square_a</span> and <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Square_b</span>, outperforming 0.71 and 0.66 of CeSD, respectively.
Furthermore, the coverage ratios of other exploration and skill discovery algorithms is significantly lower than that of our TEB. In addition, detailed comparisons of training curves can be found in Figure <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ C.3 Maze2D Experiments ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> of the Appendix <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 Learning Curves in Maze2D ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a>. In summary, the experimental results on pure exploration tasks strongly demonstrate that intrinsic rewards derived from bisimulation metrics can efficiently enhance a policy’s ability to explore unknown regions. This ability will accelerate the discovery of extrinsic rewards and promote faster policy convergence in practical tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18724v1/figures/ablation_all.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/108;" width="476" height="108" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation Studies. <span id="S4.F4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left</span>: the three figures show the ablation curves of TEB components across three tasks; <span id="S4.F4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right</span>: the fourth figure illustrates the ablation results regarding anchor state selection for intrinsic rewards across the three tasks. Each task is run for 1M steps with three random seeds. Note that for better performance comparison, the anchor ablation experiment (right) exhibits the episode success rate at 50% of the training steps.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ C.5 Exploration Visualizations in Maze2D ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, We also visualize state coverage over 100K training steps by rendering whether each discretized spatial bin of the maze map has been visited. We only show representative tasks for partial baselines, and more visualizations are available in the Appendix <a href="#A3.SS5" title="C.5 Exploration Visualizations in Maze2D ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a>.
Overall, the visualization comparisons intuitively show that TEB achieved the highest map coverage, which qualitatively validates its strongest exploration ability. Specifically, most baselines can only explore areas near the initial state, typically stalling at turns, such as LBS and RND in the <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Square_a</span> and <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Square_tree</span> map. Moreover, compared with the strong CeSD baseline, TEB maintains deep exploration while also stably expanding into the surrounding regions around newly discovered states, such as the <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Square_tree</span> map. These properties indicate that metric-based intrinsic rewards do not prematurely drive value convergence and cause policy stagnation, but instead provide a stable incentive that sustains effective exploration throughout training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TEB Components.</span>
This ablation study analyzes the effectiveness of predictive bisimulation metric-based representation learning (labeled “Rep”) and metric-based intrinsic reward (“Int”) in TEB. Therefore, we progressively remove components (“TEB w/o Rep”, “TEB w/o Rep &amp; Int”) and also plug our representation module into ICM and CeSD (“ICM w/ Rep”, “CeSD w/ Rep”). As depicted in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Reward-free Maze2D Experiments ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we observe several intuitive results. (1) Comparing the first three variants in the figure, both the representation module and the intrinsic module provide non-trivial gains on all tasks except <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Box-close</span>, which validates the effectiveness of each component. (2) Comparing TEB against powerful “ICM w/ Rep” and “CeSD w/ Rep”, we find that even under a unified metric-based representation backbone, TEB still achieves the best overall performance, which also shows the effectiveness of our intrinsic module and implies the systematic gains from the task-aware exploration. (3) Comparing the last four, plugging our representation into ICM and CeSD consistently improves their performance, suggesting that the module is broadly beneficial.
These results provide strong evidence that both the representation and intrinsic reward components of TEB are individually effective and more importantly, yield powerful performance when coupled within a metric-based framework.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Anchor State Selection.</span>
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Reward-free Maze2D Experiments ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the right bar chart reports the episode success rate of the three selection strategies of anchor states. Our TEB with the pseudo-anchor state outperforms both the (“TEB w/ Random”) with random anchor states and the (“TEB w/ <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>”) with fixed initial-state anchors, i.e., <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, across all tasks, especially in <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Pick-out-of-hole</span>. Furthermore, we directly observe that suboptimal random anchor strategy (random permutations from batches) is slightly better than the fixed initial anchor strategy, but not significantly. Overall, these results highlight that the anchor selection is critical, and demonstrates the superiority of our anchor strategy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Effectiveness of Predicted Gaussian Rewards</h3>

<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18724v1/figures/effe_r.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/138;" width="476" height="138" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance analysis of the bisimulation metric with different reward signals.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.5 Effectiveness of Predicted Gaussian Rewards ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we consider two metric-based representations without intrinsic exploration based on TEB, where the internal reward differentials (in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 The Proposed Predictive Bisimulation Metric ‣ 3 Method ‣ Task-Aware Exploration via a Predictive Bisimulation Metric" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>)) use predicted Gaussian rewards and ground-truth rewards from environments, respectively. Comparative results across three tasks show that our metric-based representations with predicted rewards significantly outperform the traditional environment rewards on most tasks. Furthermore, the “TEB w/o Int” curve reveals that the predicted method can learn quickly. In summary, combined with the TEB curve, the final results indicate that the performance improvement of TEB stems not only from the predicted Gaussian reward but also from the downstream metric-based intrinsic reward, which provides a considerable performance boost.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning has made notable progress in intrinsic exploration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pathak et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazzaglia et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Early approaches like the intrinsic curiosity module <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pathak et al., 2017</a>)</cite> promote exploration by leveraging dynamic prediction error. The CIC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laskin et al., 2022</a>)</cite> introduces a contrastive objective to maximize the mutual information between latent skills and resulting trajectories. The recent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2024</a>)</cite> diversifies skills using policy ensembles regularized by entropy constraints, while preserving behavioral consistency. Variants like DVFB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite> enables skill discovery with strong generalization by aligning policies across time. However, most of these methods are tested in low-dimensional <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, highly task-specific tasks and are often difficult to extend to visual tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laskin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Visual RL under sparse rewards remains challenging due to the both variations and the weak reward signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yarats et al., 2021b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mete et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Most recent work focuses on visual representation learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee and Hwang, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with limited efforts by coupled it with reward explorations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yarats et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>. Specifically, the methods widely adopt bisimulation metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, mutual information maximization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and contrastive augmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laskin et al., 2020</a>)</cite> to learn task-relevant latent spaces. DrM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> boosts representation and exploration via neuron activation, but its task-agnostic bonus demands careful hyperparameter tuning. More recently, spectral representation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> leverages spectral decomposition of the transition operator to capture compact dynamic features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have introduced a task-aware exploration framework (TEB) that tightly couples visual representation and exploration through a robust predictive bisimulation metric. TEB keeps the metric non-degenerate using predicted Gaussian rewards under sparse rewards, and then builds an effective metric-based intrinsic reward to drive task-aware global exploration without changing the optimal policy. Experiments on challenging MetaWorld and Maze2D show TEB significantly boosts the exploration ability and policy performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">In <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_inbook">UAI</span>,
</span>
